title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Introduction
content: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and ankylosing spondylitis (AS) are among the most common rheumatic diseases. These chronic progressive inflammatory diseases lead to a reduction in physical fitness and an increase in joint degeneration. [1] Although they are very closely related, their symptomatology and etiology differ. In the past, AS was often diagnosed inaccurately as RA, but the two have recently been recognized as separate, distinct clinical entities. The latter has been attributed to advancing diagnostic and laboratory techniques that differentiate the two conditions. [2] Diagnostic differentiation remains a challenging task for clinicians.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Introduction
content: The presenting symptoms, radiographic characteristics, and serological testing can similarly characterize RA and AS. However, RA and AS have widely different characteristics, with distinct pathophysiology and underlying genetic parameters for each. [3] [4] This makes the probability of a patient having both conditions rather low. The diagnosis can be challenging because the two have similar clinical manifestations, such as changes in radiography or peripheral/morning stiffness, and more tests may be required to establish the correct etiology. [5] Furthermore, the authors have reported cases of coexisting AS and RA since 1976. [6]

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Various studies have suggested that rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and ankylosing spondylitis (AS) have overlapping etiologies. [7] These suggestions are based on the different genetic backgrounds that contribute to the development of conditions in a patient. Suppose a patient has human leukocyte antigen (HLA) HLA-DR4 of RA and the predisposing HLA-B27 of AS simultaneously and is affected by an environmental agent. In that case, there is a chance of RA and AS coexistence. [8] The first case of simultaneous RA and AS was reported in 1976. Since that first report, fewer than 60 such cases have been reported. [9] This underreporting can be attributed to a lack of clinical examination, observation, or comprehensive evaluation.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: The frequency of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and ankylosing spondylitis (AS) in the general population ranges between 0.3% and 1.5%.[9] AS is more common in males, and RA is more common in females. AS-associated symptoms show before the age of 30, but RA happens later, between 40 and 50.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: Studies estimate that 90% of patients with RA develop cervical spondylitis. RA cervical spondylitis has presented with classic patterns of instability, including atlantoaxial subluxation, subaxial subluxation, and basilar invagination. The latter occurs in about 20% of RA patients [10] .

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: Globally, prevalence varies depending on the ethnic group and the prevalence of human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27. The prevalence of AS is approximately 5% to 6% among people who are HLA-B27-positive. [11]

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Epidemiological data cite that both rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and ankylosing spondylitis (AS) have hereditary predilections. Certain families and identical twins emphasize the importance of genetic factors (a 60% association in RA), but environmental factors also play a significant role.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: In RA cases, HLA-DR4 and HLA-DR1 are considered essential genetic backgrounds. This is particularly true among smokers with a positive anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP). HLA-B27 is the strongest genetic association of AS (first reported in 1973), but HLA-DRB1 has also been linked to this disease. HLA-B27 is not associated with RA.

content: Genetic predisposition and environmental factors initiate an autoimmune reaction, and antibodies target the synovium and soft tissue, leading to inflammation and the gradual destruction of the organs.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Symmetrical inflammation of various joints of the hands and feet (metacarpophalangeal, proximal interphalangeal, wrist, and metatarsophalangeal joints) is the most common initial manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The feeling of morning stiffness often lasts more than an hour. As the disease progresses, erosion happens, leading to the characteristic deformation of the fingers and toes. [12]

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- History and Physical -- Rheumatoid Spondylitis
content: Diagnostic criteria for RA include inflammatory arthritis involving three or more joints that lasts more than 6 weeks, a positive rheumatoid factor (RF), and/or anti-citrullinated peptide/protein antibody testing. Inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) or the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), can be elevated, and symptoms cannot be attributed to other pathologies, including psoriatic arthritis, acute viral polyarthritis, polyarticular gout, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, or systemic lupus erythematosus.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- History and Physical -- Rheumatoid Spondylitis
content: Patients with RA who develop cervical spondylitis can present with occipital headaches secondary to compression of the greater occipital branch of the C2 nerve, which occurs secondary to degeneration of the C1-C2 joint. A classic grading system that has been utilized to categorize the severity of neurologic impairment with RA spondylitis is the Ranawat Classification System: Grade I: Subjective paresthesias, pain Grade II: Subjective weakness, upper motor neuron findings Grade III: Objective weakness, upper motor neuron findings IIIA: Ambulatory IIIB: Nonambulatory

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- History and Physical -- Ankylosing Spondylitis
content: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is typically classified as an axial spondyloarthropathy, primarily presenting with chronic back pain and bilateral, severe arthritis of the sacroiliac joints and lumbosacral spine. Back pain is severe and starts before the age of 40. It is insidious in onset, improves with exercise but not with rest, and worsens at night. AS can lead to disabling spinal fusion and hyperkyphosis. Peripheral arthritis occurs in approximately one-third of cases. If they occur, changes are asymmetric and typically involve one large joint, such as the hip, knee, or shoulder. Erosion is rare. [11] [14]

content: Axial spondyloarthritis consists of AS and non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, characterized by symptoms of spinal inflammation and other features shared with spondyloarthritis in general. [15] [16] [17] [18]

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) happens at a younger age and involves the sacroiliac joints in an HLA-B27-positive male patient. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) cases usually involve middle-aged females with symmetrical small hand and wrist joint involvement. Tests for ESR, CRP, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibody, HLA-B27, HLA-DR2, and HLA-DR4 are all helpful in diagnosis. The first of these is nonspecific. [19] Plain X-rays show sacroiliitis in axial AS and most patients with non-axial AS. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals bone edema and more subtle changes associated with inflammation. [20] AS and RF can coexist; however, some studies have indicated that erosion polyarthritis is absent among AS patients with a positive rheumatoid factor test. [21]

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: The treatment of both groups follows a somewhat similar algorithm, although individualized treatment is the ultimate goal. The level of disease activity, the presence of poor prognostic factors or concomitant illnesses, functional impairment, the patient's tolerance of medication, the risk of adverse effects, the expectations of treatment, and other psychosocial factors must be considered. [22]

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: NSAIDS and pain medication are usually the first choice and can be given for weeks to months. Exercise and physical therapy can benefit all individuals and help prevent long-term joint stiffness, damage, and functional impairment. Traditional biologics such as methotrexate, Leflunomide, and sulfasalazine are effective in RA but not AS. Anti-tumor necrosis factor agents are effective in AS. Systemic glucocorticoids are best avoided, especially in the long term. [23]

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Surgical interventions are tailored to individual patients. Fusion of the atlantoaxial joint of the cervical spine is needed if there is significant neck or occipital pain or evidence of neurologic dysfunction due to C1-C2 subluxation, as occurs in patients with rheumatoid arthritis but not AS. Joint replacement might be needed. [23]

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Axial AS patients may also have peripheral arthritis, enthesitis, and dactylitis, which can lead to a wrong diagnosis of RA.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: Both diseases are chronic and can be managed over time for years before fatal complications happen. Many of the symptoms can be effectively controlled via medical and surgical means. The risk of cardiovascular diseases is increased in both entities, possibly secondary to the generalized inflammation. Therefore, many of these patients suffer or pass away prematurely from cardiac causes, not necessarily RA and AS. [24] [25] [26]

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Rheumatoid spondylitis in elective surgery: Any patient with RA should have flexion/extension films before having elective surgery RA spondylitis most commonly affects the occipitoatlantoaxial joint Ranawat grade IIIB patients (nonambulatory) have high associated morbidity when it comes to performing surgical intervention -- thus, the literature is very controversial concerning the use of surgery in this unique subset of RA spondylitis patients.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis are common yet distinct chronic inflammatory diseases that share overlapping clinical features, making accurate diagnosis challenging. Rheumatoid arthritis typically presents with symmetric small joint involvement in middle-aged women, while ankylosing spondylitis often affects younger men with axial spine inflammation. Each condition involves unique genetic predispositions—HLA-DR4 in rheumatoid arthritis and HLA-B27 in ankylosing spondylitis—and exhibits different responses to pharmacologic therapies. Misclassification can delay appropriate treatment, increase the risk of complications, and negatively impact quality of life. This continuing education activity enhances clinician competence in differentiating these diseases, interpreting diagnostic tests, and applying individualized management strategies.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal care for rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis requires coordinated interprofessional collaboration. Physicians and advanced practitioners must accurately diagnose and tailor treatment to the specific disease and severity. Nurses play a key role in patient education, symptom monitoring, and follow-up care. Pharmacists contribute by managing complex medication regimens and monitoring for adverse effects. Physical therapists help preserve mobility and function. Through strategic communication, shared decision-making, and coordinated care plans, the team enhances patient-centered outcomes, minimizes risks, and supports long-term disease control.
